findings.title: Request and response bodies are buffered whole with no size limit and no option to impose one
findings.impact: None demonstrated and none claimed: a Go HTTP handler that reads its own body has the same property, and bounding the body is conventionally the consumer's job through http.MaxBytesReader. The note is that this library takes over body handling from the consumer and then provides no place to express the bound, and its README never tells the consumer to add one - so the quickstart path buffers without limit by construction.
findings.evidence:
Every body path reads to EOF with no cap, and the public surface offers no way to set one:
  openapi3filter/validate_request.go:276  data, err = io.ReadAll(req.Body)
  openapi3filter/validate_request.go:453  data, err = io.ReadAll(input.Request.Body)   (a second full copy, for AuthenticationFunc)
  openapi3filter/validate_response.go:131 data, err := io.ReadAll(body)
  openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go:1420 PlainBodyDecoder
  openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go:1477 UrlencodedBodyDecoder
  openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go:1675 FileBodyDecoder
openapi3filter/options.go declares fifteen Options fields and none of them bounds a body. On the response side the middleware buffers the entire response in memory before validating it (middleware.go:195 io.MultiWriter into wr.body for the warn wrapper, :256 wr.body.Write for the strict wrapper), which also defeats streaming for any response the w

findings.title: Compiled regular expressions are cached in a package-global map that is never evicted
findings.impact: None demonstrated and none claimed. In the normal case - one process, a fixed set of documents - the map is bounded by the specifications the operator ships. In a process that loads many documents it did not author, memory grows monotonically with the number of distinct pattern strings those documents contain, and the growth is keyed on attacker-supplied text.
findings.evidence:
Every distinct `pattern` string ever compiled is stored forever in a package-level sync.Map:

  openapi3/schema.go:46      compiledPatterns sync.Map
  openapi3/schema_pattern.go:36  compiledPatterns.Store(pattern, cp)

The key is the pattern text, the value is the compiled matcher, and no code path deletes from the map - `grep -n compiledPatterns openapi3/*.go` returns only the declaration, one Load at schema.go:2727 and this Store. The cache is global rather than per-document or per-loader, so it is shared across every document a process ever loads. schema_pattern.go:15 already records that the surrounding code is racy with respect to writes to schema.Pattern.

findings.title: ZipFileBodyDecoder expands archive entries with no size or entry-count limit
findings.impact: None demonstrated and none claimed here: the decoder is opt-in and its risk is documented at the point of use. Recorded because a consumer that registers it inherits a body-to-memory amplification with no ceiling, and because the accompanying warning offers no safe alternative.
findings.evidence:
The decoder buffers the compressed body, then appends every entry's decompressed bytes into one slice with no ceiling:

  1684 func ZipFileBodyDecoder(body io.Reader, ...) (any, error) {
  1686   size, err := io.Copy(buff, body)
  1691   zr, err := zip.NewReader(bytes.NewReader(buff.Bytes()), size)
  1697   content := make([]byte, 0, bufferSize*len(zr.File))
  1700   for _, f := range zr.File {
  1713       content = append(content, buffer[:n]...)

Neither the total decompressed size nor the number of entries is bounded, so the compression ratio of the input decides the allocation. The preallocation at :1697 is itself proportional to the attacker-chosen entry count. The hazard is stated in the function's own doc comment at :1683 ('Use with caution as this implementation may be susceptible to a zip bomb attack'), and the decoder is not registered by default - the init at :1402-1417 regist

findings.title: Cross-type $ref backtrack callback panics the loader on a crafted OpenAPI document
findings.impact: Any process that loads an OpenAPI document it did not author dies on a document of this shape: openapi3.Loader offers no recover, and grep confirms none exists anywhere in the module. That covers this repository's own cmd/validate, and any service, linter, gateway, diff tool or documentation portal that accepts a user-supplied specification. Where the load happens inside a net/http handler the panic is recovered per connection; where it happens at startup, in a worker, or in a CLI, the process terminates.

findings.title: SchemaError.Error() panics instead of degrading when the rejected value cannot be JSON-encoded
findings.impact: An unauthenticated remote client turns a routine 400-class validation failure into a Go panic, deterministically and with a two-byte body - no map-ordering luck, unlike F-001. Because the panic fires while the consumer is logging or encoding the error, it can land outside whatever recover the request path has. Under net/http the request is aborted and the connection closed; off that path, the process terminates.
findings.evidence:
Rendering a validation error re-encodes the rejected value and panics if the encoder refuses it:

  3192 if !SchemaErrorDetailsDisabled {
  3193   buf.WriteString("\nSchema:\n  ")
  3194   encoder := json.NewEncoder(buf)
  3196   if err := encoder.Encode(err.Schema); err != nil { panic(err) }
  3199   buf.WriteString("\nValue:\n  ")
  3200   if err := encoder.Encode(err.Value); err != nil { panic(err) }

SchemaErrorDetailsDisabled is false by default (schema.go:34), so the branch is live out of the box.
The value reaching err.Value is not restricted to JSON-decoded types. openapi3filter registers YamlBodyDecoder for application/yaml and application/x-yaml (req_resp_decoder.go:1412-1413), and visitJSON carries a dedicated branch for the YAML decoder's non-JSON map type:

  2023 case map[any]any: // for YAML cf. issue .../issues/444
  2024   values := make(map[string]any, len(value))
  202

findings.title: CI executes third-party tooling resolved at @latest in jobs that export GITHUB_TOKEN and declare no permissions block
findings.impact: A compromise of any of these upstreams - the x/tools module, the incu6us/goimports-reviser module, or any of the five tagged actions - executes attacker code inside a job that has the repository checked out, has GITHUB_TOKEN in its environment, and in one case is explicitly invoked with a flag that rewrites source files. The blast radius reaches from tampering with the tree that later releases are cut from, up to whatever the effective token permissions allow.
findings.evidence:
The build-and-test job exports the token to every step in the job:

    8   env:
   10     GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

and `grep -rn permissions .github/workflows/` returns nothing, so both jobs inherit the repository default rather than declaring least privilege (INF-15).
In that same job, and in the second job, code fetched from a mutable @latest reference is downloaded and executed against the checked-out tree:

  128   - run: go run -a github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/cmd/validate@latest -- openapi3/testdata/test.openapi.yml
  202   - run: go install github.com/incu6us/goimports-reviser/v3@latest

findings.title: External $ref resolution reads any URL or local path with no scheme or host policy and no client timeout
findings.impact: A crafted OpenAPI document makes the loading process issue GET requests from its own network position - cloud instance metadata, internal admin interfaces, anything reachable from the host - and read arbitrary local files into the parsed document, from where their contents can surface in validation errors, in a re-serialised document, or in a diff. Denial of service through a hanging fetch is available with no crafting at all.

findings.title: Unchecked map type assertion in deepSet panics on deepObject query parameters that mix depths
findings.impact: An unauthenticated remote client aborts request validation with a Go panic on demand. Under a standard net/http server the panic is recovered per connection, so the effect is an aborted request, a closed connection and a stack trace written to the server log on every attempt - a cheap log-flooding and availability primitive. Where ValidateRequest runs outside the http handler goroutine - a worker goroutine, a gRPC gateway, a serverless handler, a CLI, or any framework that does not recover - the process terminates.

findings.title: An AWS access key identifier is tracked in a third-party test fixture
findings.impact: None: an access key identifier is not a credential on its own, the presigned signature it belongs to expired in 2017, and the document is a vendored example specification rather than this project's own configuration. Recorded because supply-chain-secrets-malware.md §8 applies to every repository and a credential-shaped string in the tree should be named rather than silently passed over, and because a scanner run by a downstream consumer will flag it again.
findings.evidence: A scan of the whole tree for high-precision secret formats (`ghp_`, `AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}`, `sk-ant-`, PEM private-key headers, `xox[baprs]-`) returned exactly one hit: a presigned S3 URL inside a third-party OpenAPI example document, carrying `X-Amz-Credential=[REDACTED:secret]/20170728/us-west-2/s3/aws4_request` together with `X-Amz-Date=20170728T...`, `X-Amz-Expires=3600` and an `X-Amz-Signature`. A second scan for `(password|secret|api[_-]?key|token)\s*[:=]\s*"..."` across non-test Go files returned nothing. The value is an AWS access key identifier, not a secret access key; the signature it accompanies expired one hour after 2017-07-28.

findings.title: The encoded-path-separator gate is enforced by ValidationHandler and not by the Validator middleware
findings.impact: Where it lands, the security requirements and the parameter and body schema of one operation are enforced while a different operation is served: an operation whose spec declares no `security` can be validated in place of one that does, which is an authorization bypass rather than a validation gap. Where the two routers happen to agree, there is no effect.

advisories_to_match.summary: kin-openapi has uncontrolled resource consumption in openapi3filter deepObject query parameter decoding
advisories_to_match.description:
### Summary

An uncontrolled resource consumption vulnerability in `openapi3filter` lets any unauthenticated client force multi-gigabyte heap allocation with a single, tiny HTTP request. When a spec declares a `deepObject`-style query parameter whose schema contains an array (a normal, documented pattern), the decoder reconstructs the array by reading the **largest attacker-supplied index** and allocating one slot for every position from `0` up to that index — *before* schema validation (including `maxItems`) ever runs. A request as small as 24 bytes (`?param[items][50000000]=x`) drives heap allocation to **~6.1 GiB**, reliably triggering an OOM kill / restart loop on memory-constrained services.

### Details

The OpenAPI `style: deepObject` serialization lets clients express arrays in the query string using bracket notation, e.g. `param[items][0]=a&param[items][1]=b`. The decoder first collects these into an intermediate `map[string]any` keyed by the string of the index, then converts that sparse map into a real `[]any` in [`sliceMapToSlice`](https://github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/blob/master/openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go#L936):

advisories_to_match.summary: kin-openapi openai3filter: nil-pointer panic in ConvertErrors on malformed multipart/form-data body enables unauthenticated DoS
advisories_to_match.description:
### Summary

A nil-pointer dereference in `openapi3filter.ConvertErrors` lets any unauthenticated client crash a server with a single HTTP request. When an application validates a `multipart/form-data` request body and renders the resulting validation error through the library-provided `ValidationErrorEncoder` / `ConvertErrors` helpers, a malformed scalar form field (e.g. a non-numeric value for an `integer` property) produces an error shape that `convertParseError` dereferences without a nil check. The handler goroutine panics, causing a denial of service. `application/json` request bodies are **not** affected — the bug is specific to `multipart/form-data`.

### Details

The panic is in `convertParseError`, at [`openapi3filter/validation_error_encoder.go:119-120`](https://github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/blob/master/openapi3filter/validation_error_encoder.go#L119) (still present on `master` at the time of writing):
